title: An open letter to every family’s designated IT support
author: Mozilla
article_text: Almost every family has one. They’re the only ones who know which remote turns on the TV and which controls the volume and channels. They know what an HDMI cable actually does and where to plug it in. They’ve even fixed multiple phone issues within seconds through a little-known, well-kept secret procedure (turning it off and back on). Perhaps they are a parent, tech-savvy sibling, cool aunt or uncle, or close family friend. Whatever the relation, the role stays the same. They are the unpaid, on-call tech specialist for every relative’s forgotten password, printer jam, and device settings update. If this sounds like you, we would first like to thank you for doing a job you never signed up for. Second, we would like to share a simple way you can help your family and friends protect their privacy and security without adding more to your plate. With Android and iPhone’s latest releases, and Black Friday deals rapidly approaching, many people are upgrading their current phone to a newer model. As the family’s go-to tech helper, you’ll likely be setting up a few new devices in the near future. You already know the routine: connect to Wi-Fi, choose a language, and transfer data from the old phone to the new one. But beyond the steps you are prompted to take when setting up a new phone lies a quiet decision many people never think twice about: their default browser. While people in some regions, like Europe and Japan, get to choose their default browser when setting up a new phone, this is not the case everywhere. Most phones ship with a browser preinstalled and set as the default, ready to start collecting data and monetizing off user activity the minute it’s opened. Unless deliberately changed, that’s the browser that will be used moving forward. Not because it’s the best option, but because it’s already there. But remember, everyone can choose the browser they use, and as the designated tech whiz of the family, you can help inspire others to choose the right one. Choosing Firefox means choosing privacy from the very first tap. A browser is the door to everything you do online, and depending on how it’s designed, it can see a lot. Every site visited. Every phrase searched. Every link tapped. As we socialize, work, and explore on our phones, the browser can be the biggest funnel of personal data leaving that device, and how it’s built determines who collects that data, who can sell it, and how long it sticks around. Privacy is the starting point for our browser, not an afterthought. Firefox is built on the principle that not even Mozilla should know which websites you visit or what you do there. Firefox is backed by Mozilla, a nonprofit-backed company with no shareholders to report to. Instead of chasing financial returns for a small group, Mozilla aims to provide an internet that truly puts people first. This means we limit the data we know about you and give you more choice about what data you share and when. This commitment to user privacy is built into the browser itself. On both Android and iOS, Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) is enabled by default, blocking known trackers every time you browse. This helps prevent advertisers and data brokers from following people across sites, no setup required. You can also adjust ETP to fit different needs, including turning it off altogether or activating Strict mode for even stronger protection. Control and choice are built in, too. Firefox has an easily accessible AI controls section where people can customize how AI features show up in the browser, or turn them off entirely – because AI should always be a choice, not a requirement. To carry these principles and protections across every link opened on a new phone, set Firefox as the default mobile browser in just a few taps. Downloading the Firefox mobile app isn’t enough on its own, since most phones will keep opening links in whatever browser came preinstalled unless told otherwise. Here’s how to make Firefox the browser that actually opens by default. Make sure Firefox is installed on the device you’re working with before you begin.On Android: On iOS: Once Firefox has been selected as the default browser, links tapped from messages, email, social media, or anywhere else will open in Firefox automatically. No additional steps required by your less tech-savvy family members and friends, and no relying on them to open the “right” browser every time they want to access the internet. The way a device is initially set up tends to stick. Whichever browser is already selected as default and whatever privacy settings are (or aren’t) adjusted on day one often just…stay that way. That’s a lot of reliance on whatever defaults the phone is purchased with. So this fall, whether you are setting up a shiny new Google Pixel 11 for your aunt, an iPhone 18 Pro for your brother, or any other model for any one of your non-paying tech support “clients,” take an extra five minutes to help them download Firefox and set it as their default browser. They can start their new device journey browsing with privacy, choice, and control built in. And you can check one more thing off your unofficial family IT to-do list.

title: Firefox’s free built-in VPN uncaps data limit through January 2027
author: Mozilla
article_text: Whether you’re heading home to see family this winter or taking a well-earned break before the year wraps up, we want you to browse with a little more peace of mind. That’s why, as our gift to you, everyone using Firefox’s free built-in VPN gets unlimited data starting today, November 10, through January 31, 2027. Sign in with a Mozilla account and unlock extra privacy for all that shopping, travel planning, and everyday browsing, no gift receipt required. Using Firefox’s free built-in VPN makes it harder for websites to use your IP address to determine where you are, or connect your visits across the web. Most importantly, you’re not trading your browsing data for that protection: Firefox doesn’t sell your browsing data, interrupt you with ads, or keep a record of the websites you visit. You can use VPN to: Two things to remember: Firefox’s free built-in VPN is available to people using Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS is coming soon!). To start using the service: You can check for availability in your region and review full instructions for using VPN on desktop and Android in our Help Center. Download Firefox to try it out today.

title: Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead
author: Mozilla
article_text: Some of our latest Firefox updates have had big moments of their own, from the launch of our new design and built-in ad blocking on iOS to Firefox Enterprise and our partnership with NVIDIA GeForce NOW. You might’ve even spotted a few familiar internet OGs in our latest campaign. Other improvements might’ve flown under the radar until you open a PDF or move your tabs around. We wanted to take a moment to highlight some of the features and improvements we’ve been working on, from recent additions you might have missed to a look at what’s coming next. When we launched our public roadmap in June, we shared plans to make everyday browsing more useful, flexible and private. We’ve now updated it with more of what’s ahead. We’re developing these features in the open, in close partnership with our contributors, and will share more about release timing as each feature gets ready for more people to try. Here’s a look at what’s in the works: Try the latest updates and explore the Firefox roadmap for more of what we’re working on. If there’s something you’re looking forward to, or something you’d like us to improve, tell us on Mozilla Connect. Your feedback helps shape what comes next.

title: Skip the busywork with Smart Window
author: Mozilla
article_text: The days might be getting shorter, but your to-do list is only getting longer. Whether you’re getting a head start on holiday shopping or planning your next career move, Smart Window’s newest features will help you keep up. Firefox’s opt-in AI browsing experience can now use information from tabs you choose to help fill out forms. It can also watch web pages and notify you about specific changes you’ve asked it to track. Job applications ask for your work history; event registrations ask for a professional bio. If those details are already in your open tabs, Smart Window can now use pages you choose to suggest what to enter, saving you extra clicks and some CtrlC, CtrlV. For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models. To get started, click into a form field. If the form has at least four text fields that Smart Window can help fill, you’ll see “Fill from sources” appear in the dropdown, along with a recommended source page. Select “Fill from sources” to continue, or click the pencil icon to open “Edit sources” if you want to change or add tabs. Once you’ve chosen your sources, review the suggestions before filling out the form. You can edit the results before submitting; Smart Window won’t submit the form for you. When you choose to use this feature, information from your selected source pages is shared with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model used for detecting the fields and extracting relevant information from your selected tabs. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same, and saved autofill values stay on your device. Learn more about how form filling works. This feature currently supports text fields on web forms and does not save any generated form fill data. We’re exploring support for more field types, including dropdown menus, as well as PDF forms and ways to save and manage generated information for future forms. A watched pot never boils, and refreshing a web page won’t make an update appear any sooner. Smart Window can now watch a page for a specific update, whether that’s an item going on sale or a new job listing that includes a job title or company name that you’re following. Each task can follow up to five pages, so you can keep an eye on several stores or job boards at the same time. Type “/watch” in the Smart Window chat to set up a task. Describe what you’re looking for, add the pages to watch, and choose whether Firefox should check for updates on a daily or weekly basis. Those checks run only while the browser is open. When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether. Page monitoring uses the Qwen AI model to identify changes that match what you’re looking for. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same. Learn more about creating and managing tasks. These two new features are available in the Smart Window beta on desktop, in English in the U.S. and Canada, and will roll out to additional markets in the coming months. Try Smart Window and share your experience on Mozilla Connect. We’d love to hear how you’re using Smart Window to get things done and what you’d like it to help with next.

title: Firefox reunites meme royalty to remind you what the internet used to feel like
author: Mozilla
article_text: A group of familiar faces from the early web just got back together to ask an important question: What happened to the internet? Sure, there was a time when it was a little less polished, and a lot less speedy, but it was yours. Overly Attached Girlfriend may have wanted to know everything about you, but your browser didn’t need to. Dancing Matt boogied all over the world, without any corporations tracking him or selling his personal data. And while Annoying Orange is incredibly annoying, he’s not as annoying as forced AI features. These beloved early internet personalities remind us of a time when surfing the web felt open, organic, and most importantly, personal. And good news: With Firefox, it still can. That’s why we’re teaming up with these icons to remind people what our browser offers, and show those who wandered off why now is the time to come back. For Mozilla Chief Marketing Officer John Solomon, the aim of the campaign started with winning back people who originally loved and used Firefox. “I kept going back to Firefox’s heyday, when the internet was really fun, weird, and interesting. The challenge was: how do you lean on nostalgia and heritage, but not be stuck in the past?” The campaign was created by We Believers, one of the world’s most awarded independent agencies, with production handled by nobodys and direction by the Sunny Sixteen collective. “We wanted to create an idea that truly belongs to Firefox — a challenger browser that helped shape the internet’s golden years and stayed independent as Big Tech took over. The goal? Remind former users that what they loved about Firefox matters more than ever now,” said Gustavo Lauria, Founder and CCO at We Believers. Solomon said the finished campaign achieves the goal of embracing Firefox’s history without living in it: “Our partners really cracked it. We wanted to remind people of what made the internet so wonderful in the first place. These are people who helped make it strange, creative, surprising, and fun. None of them were trying to go viral. They were normal, everyday people who were using the internet. That’s the way the internet should be and why we feel it’s a great moment for Firefox. Always independent and unlike big tech, not trying to extract more from everyday people.” Whether you used Firefox back in the day, or are simply looking for a better browsing experience, we’re still here, staying true to the values we were built on. We believe the internet should be open, accessible, and shaped by the people who use it, not just the platforms that profit from their attention and data. This means a web where you can explore without feeling tracked or used for profit, where you decide for yourself how new technology fits into your life, and you can trust that your browser protects you by default. Firefox has built-in privacy protections to help limit tracking, lets you decide if AI features appear and customize how they behave, and uses open source code that anyone can see. To learn more about what sets Firefox apart, check out five reasons to choose the browser that puts you first. We know a better internet isn’t built by finding new ways to capture your attention or information. It’s about giving you more freedom to make the web your own. The internet has changed a lot since Numa Numa Guy first danced his way into our collective memory. But the things that made it magical – creativity, curiosity, community, and the freedom to explore – are still worth protecting. Firefox has championed those values since the beginning, and we’re not giving up on them now. That’s why we’re celebrating the people who helped make the early web what it was, while reminding everyone that a more open, human internet is still an option. The early days of the internet may be behind us, but the spirit doesn’t have to be. Experience it for yourself. Now more than ever: come back to Firefox. This post is also available in: Deutsch (German) Français (French)

title: Still here, still yours: 5 reasons to choose Firefox
author: Mozilla
article_text: The internet used to feel like a community, not a commodity. Browsers were tools for exploration, and you could wander the web without feeling tracked everywhere.Today, as the web becomes increasingly surveilled and commercialized, Firefox preserves the magic, freedom, and fun of the early internet. Still open source, still independent, still privacy-focused. No billionaire owner, no hidden agenda.So, whether you’re new here, back after a break, or just curious, here are five reasons to choose the browser that puts you first. Firefox is backed by the Mozilla Foundation, a non-profit committed to an open internet. Unlike other big tech companies, we’re built with privacy as the default. Our open source code is visible, reviewable, and continuously stress-tested by a global community, truly putting power in the hands of the people it’s built for. While other browsers allow third-party trackers to profile you, Firefox’s Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) helps stop cross-site tracking before it starts, letting your browser work faster. Plus, when you sync information like history and bookmarks across devices, it’s encrypted locally, meaning only you can access it. Learn about some of our other privacy-focused features like password manager, built-in VPN, and Relay in our guide to strengthening your online security for free with Firefox. We believe the only person who should decide how you interact with AI features in your browser is you. Firefox offers a clear, easily accessible AI controls section where you can turn off AI features entirely — or decide which ones stay on depending on your workflow and preferences. For those wanting a little more help getting things done, Smart Window is Firefox’s most integrated AI experience. With your permission, its built-in, AI-powered assistant can work directly with your open tabs and browsing history to connect the dots. This means it can compare information, summarize pages, and help plan projects without requiring you to provide context from your past and current browsing activity every time you start a new prompt. Newer feature additions to Smart Window include the ability to group related tabs together and visual history previews that help you find a page you visited earlier when you can’t remember the exact URL or phrase searched. Also, our partnership with Exa enables Smart Window to find current web information to include in responses while also displaying the sources behind these answers, so you can verify what you’re seeing without interrupting your workflow. Smart Window remains in beta as we continue to learn and improve from our community’s feedback. Try it yourself here. Firefox is not built on Chromium, the open source browser project that supports Google Chrome and many other browsers. As a matter of fact, we are one of the last major browsers that isn’t. Instead, Firefox runs on Mozilla’s independent Gecko browser engine, which was developed specifically to uphold our strong privacy standards and give people more control over their data and browsing experience. This independence also impacts how Firefox handles browser add-ons, particularly ad blockers. Unlike Chromium-based browsers that now limit how powerful ad-blocking tools can be, Firefox still allows ad blockers like uBlock Origin to work at full strength. This means people who use Firefox can enjoy stronger, more reliable ad and tracker blocking without compromise, something increasingly difficult on Chromium-based browsers due to imposed limitations. Firefox is constantly building features and solutions to help you navigate the web on your own terms, and we wanted to make this support visible. Enter Kit, Firefox’s companion to the internet. Kit isn’t an AI assistant or chatbot, just a friendly face that you might see during moments that are meant to feel friendly and supportive, like when you’re just getting set up, exploring a new feature, or celebrating a win such as successfully adjusting a setting. While the internet is ever-changing, Firefox remains rooted in the values that defined its beginning. Our browser was created on the principles of privacy, independence, and choice,and we continue to uphold them as we innovate and evolve. In a web landscape dominated by profit, surveillance, and sameness, our browser preserves the open and human spirit of the early internet. New, returning, or loyal for years, there’s always a place for you here. Download Firefox and make the web yours again. This post is also available in: Deutsch (German) Français (French)

title: Why is the CMA asking us to choose the furniture before the house? The UK’s search choice screens need browser choice screens alongside them
author: Gemma Petrie
article_text: Mobile browsers are a key gateway to the internet for 56 million people in the UK. Smartphone users spend around half an hour a day in these apps, and opening a browser is the most common way they look up information online. Yet most people are using a smartphone browser that was preinstalled and set as the default for them, without ever being asked which browser they would actually prefer. Mozilla believes people deserve an active choice in the tools they depend on every day, which is why the latest proposals from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) matter. We welcome the CMA’s plans to give people a choice of search service and are asking it to consult on browser choice now, so both screens can launch together. On September 23rd, the CMA published updated plans that would require Google to show people in the UK a choice of search service on new Android devices, covering the default search app and home-screen search widget as well as Chrome. Search choice screens would also appear in Chrome on other platforms, including through a major update for existing users. Some AI assistants would also be eligible to appear alongside search engines. The CMA’s mobile browser investigation found that preinstallation, prominent placement and default settings restrict browser competition. Mozilla’s innovative 2023 experiment showed that properly designed browser choice screens can help people choose a browser they expect to keep using, and can be an effective tool for giving people agency over their online life. It also showed that an overwhelming majority of people (98%!) want to see them. The EU Digital Markets Act has since demonstrated their impact in practice. We welcome the CMA’s work on search choice, but people in the UK deserve browser choice too. Asking people to pick a search service inside a browser that most of them never actively chose in the first place leaves some of the biggest issues identified in the CMA’s own mobile browser investigation unaddressed. The CMA commissioned user research on search choice screens to refine and improve the proposals it first consulted on in January. Providers’ positions on the choice screen would be fully randomised. Users would have to scroll to the bottom before confirming, and could “test drive” a search provider for at least a week. The CMA has also recognized that search is changing. Its research found that many people were already using AI assistants to search alongside traditional search services. Under the revised, more technology-neutral eligibility criteria, an AI assistant could also qualify to appear on the search choice screen if it meets the requirements, including being able to search the web and attribute its sources. But browser choice should not be left behind. The EU’s Digital Markets Act introduced browser choice screens on iOS for the first time and brought browser and search choice together during Android set-up. Browser first, then search, so the relationship between the two makes sense. In Japan, search and browser choice screens are presented on both Android and iOS. And people are making use of the browser screen to select alternatives. In May, we reported Firefox is selected through a DMA choice screen once every ten seconds, with retention five times higher than for organic downloads. Other independent browsers have also reported substantial growth. The CMA’s proposals recognize that AI is changing how people search. AI is also changing what browsers offer, adding to the ways they compete on features, privacy and user control. Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar, and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters. When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too. We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service. Mozilla’s response to the consultation is available here.

title: This map shows the most important asset that VC-backed companies need right now
author: Mark Surman
article_text: What’s the most vital asset for an AI company today? For venture backed AI business, it might be “funding” or “revenue”. But, there’s another asset that’s just as critical: trust. At Mozilla, building technology that people and businesses can genuinely trust has been a long-standing, guiding principle. That’s why we’re supporting the launch of the Trustworthy AI Map, a market map of VC-backed companies building the infrastructure for trustworthy AI. Supported by seven organizations, including Mozilla, the Trustworthy AI Map features 79 companies across 15 countries, from early to later-stage venture. It maps companies building products for AI deployment across seven layers of the AI stack, including identity, data control, interoperability and evaluation. The map connects the products with the companies and capital behind them, helping investors, founders and businesses explore commercial opportunities. To be featured, trust must be baked into its product or business model through human agency, trust by design or aligned business models. This initiative aligns with much of our work over the past year. We’ve invested in companies through Mozilla Ventures, launched Otari, an open source enterprise tool which allows you to control your LLM infrastructure from a single layer, and published landmark research in our State of Open Source AI report that’s demystifying the open source AI landscape and shows that the capability gap between open and closed models is closing. We’ve also partnered with Mila: the Quebec AI Institute, to build an open source AI foundation layer that enables organizations and institutions to own and operate their own advanced AI systems locally, ensuring full control over their technology and data. The project has the backing of the Canadian government, and industry leaders like Hypertec. At a time when fear and uncertainty about AI are on the rise, trust is not just a virtue; it’s a path towards profitability. Explore the Trustworthy AI Map to see how. Learn more at trustworthyaimap.org.

title: What does the (Fire)fox say?
author: Mozilla
article_text: It all started with a question: What does Firefox sound like to you?Over the past year, Mozilla developed a small but meaningful set of sounds to add a sonic dimension to the Firefox experience. When we started this process, we knew we wanted something warm, human, and representative of our open source identity. We also knew we didn’t want to invent these sounds in a vacuum. So we did what we’ve always done and turned to our community.With the help of creative audio company Sounds Like These, we reached out to Firefox users, contributors, and team members across the globe asking them to send us audio and written descriptions of what Firefox sounds like to them. This feedback became our compass.From there, we began building three new sounds that bring to life our logo, mascot Kit, and Firefox notifications. The logo and Kit sound have already begun rolling out across the Firefox brand (check them out in our new design launch announcement) – and we’re excited to bring the notification sound to the browser in a future update.Not only did we want these new sounds to reflect Mozilla’s mission and values, we also wanted to ensure they felt connected to one another. This is the story of how they came to be. Because Mozilla uses a community-based approach to create world-class open source software, we wanted Firefox’s audio logo to share this same spirit. This meant creating something built by many and rooted in real human experience.Inspired by early community feedback that associated Firefox with nature, we started with delicate organic textures, including bird song and the thump of wood being struck to evoke the feeling of Kit moving through different environments. We also knew we wanted to utilize the voices of real Mozilla employees, or “Mozillians.” As Sounds Like These Co-founder Sam Heath reflected, “What better way to represent the brand than the sound of the people behind it?”At first, we considered setting up a professional recording session in a large city where multiple Mozillians could drop in to be recorded. However, we quickly realized this would limit the voices we would be able to include to one geographic location. It was then suggested: Why not just let people record wherever they are? After all, Firefox is used in family living rooms, shared offices, and really most places one can access the internet.The final result includes the voices of 23 real Mozillians saying “Firefox!”, in which you can hear their subtle differences in accent, tone, and timing. Sam shared that some of these employee submissions included the echoes of distant chatter, families, and all the other subtle sounds of Mozillians’ real life playing out as they recorded. He explained that Sounds Like These did not deliberately edit out the entirety of this ambient sound to preserve the texture and authenticity that comes from real people living their real lives.“That was something that was very clear from Mozilla from the start. We don’t want to be this shiny, distracting tech brand. We wanted this to feel real, natural, and human,” said Sam. Kit holds the prestigious title of VP of Mascoting at Firefox, and we worked hard to ensure their sound properly reflects such an important position. Kit’s not an AI assistant, nor a chatbot. They’re not an actual fox, or a red panda either. They’re a Firefox, its own creature not of this world. Kit may appear in your Firefox browser during moments that are meant to feel welcoming and encouraging, like when you’re getting started, trying out a new feature, or successfully making a settings change. Our goal when creating the Kit sound was to convey Kit’s friendly, familiar, and trustworthy presence without mimicking any real animal. The sound had to be flexible enough to express movement and emotion across animations and videos, while also remaining instantly recognizable.Early experiments ranged from pure animal sounds to abstract musical expressions. Foxes were considered, but as Sam noted, “Foxes are incredibly difficult to record, and they do make cute sounds, but never around people. You only really seem to hear them literally screaming – and we definitely didn’t want anyone screaming.”We also explored a more feline route, specifically a cat purr. As Oli Slack, Co-Founder and Head of Audio at Sounds Like These, explains, “The cat purr was almost kind of perfect…other than the fact that it sounded just like a cat purring. So we asked, ‘How do we recreate the feeling of what the purr sounds like, without it being an actual cat purr?’”This is where the process really got interesting. While brainstorming cat purr alternatives, the Sounds Like These team researched the psychology behind what makes certain sounds more comforting and familiar. Soft tones and warmth from other humans instinctively register as more reassuring and honest, and this also crosses over into animals, particularly animals we keep as companions. This validated our initial draw toward the cat purr, and confirmed we were heading in the right direction sonically.The breakthrough came when Sounds Like These stopped looking at animal sounds as a starting point, instead using a human voice as the basis of a custom purr. This wasn’t someone imitating a cat or “purring” themselves, it served as a foundation vocalization that was then uniquely shaped and layered to convey Kit’s friendly and encouraging presence. And thus, the Kit sound was born. Notifications don’t have to be jarring or intrusive, and that’s exactly what we wanted to avoid when creating one for Firefox.Our new notification sound – which we look forward to rolling out in a future Firefox update – was carefully crafted to gently alert, not interrupt. It draws inspiration from community feedback that described the feeling of using Firefox like a door opening and referenced moments of quiet discovery filled with gentle wonderment and joy.This sense of seamless exploration is reflected in the sound’s design: a soft whoosh, like a door swinging open, followed by a subtle click, all in an airy, rounded tone to feel helpful, not demanding.The result is a sound that softly notifies rather than disrupts or controls, staying true to the feeling of joyful curiosity that many users associate with browsing the web through Firefox. From the very beginning of this process, we leaned into Mozilla’s values of openness and community.We consulted our fans and team members. We used real voices. We embraced the imperfections of being human.These sounds are now a part of Firefox’s story, and we hope every time you hear them, they remind you that you’re using a browser built by the people, for the people.

title: Mozilla introduces Firefox Enterprise
author: Mozilla
article_text: Institutions are recalculating who controls the technology they rely on. Mozilla has an independent option to offer. For years, organizations consolidated technology around a small number of providers to make things simpler. Fewer systems. Tighter integrations. More economies of scale. But that consolidation went well beyond technology. It consolidated dependency, too. The resulting risks have been debated, studied, and challenged along the way, but concentration continued. More work, data and critical infrastructure kept moving to the same few providers, while credible alternatives narrowed.The deeper that dependency runs, the harder and more costly it becomes to change course. When something fails, changes or falls outside an institution’s control, that dependency becomes a risk for CIOs and CISOs to manage. Nowhere are these stakes more visible than in Europe. Now institutions are re-assessing. Governments are pushing for greater digital autonomy, while regulated industries face growing pressure to find and manage their dependencies. There’s a name for much of this debate about technological control: “sovereignty.” What digital sovereignty means in practice varies. Across Europe, governments are investing in the security and resilience of critical IT infrastructure, reducing strategic dependencies and putting technological autonomy higher on national agendas. Different approaches, same underlying concern. Strip away the regional policy definitions and industry distinctions and a pretty practical, universal question emerges: how much technological dependency should we risk? And a very specific, very important layer has been largely missing from that conversation: the browser. The browser. Applications run there. Employees authenticate in it. Sensitive data transits through it. Files are uploaded and downloaded and AI tools are increasingly used through it. That raises the same questions of dependency and control: whose browser technology are you relying on, and who controls the infrastructure used to manage it? Firefox Enterprise is built for organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance requirements. It pairs the Firefox browser, built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, with a management console organizations can run on their own infrastructure. From that console, IT teams can centrally manage browser policy and access, govern how data moves through the browser and set controls around AI use. IT and security teams get more control over their data, IT infrastructure and browser environment — helping strengthen technological independence and operational resilience. “If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” said Anthony Enzor-DeMeo, CEO of Mozilla. “We built Firefox differently. And we’re bringing its independent architecture to institutions that are ready to rethink their dependencies and risk.” We’re starting with the browser because we see it as a key, but under-governed, layer. Firefox Enterprise gives institutions more control over the browser and the infrastructure managing it. And because Firefox runs on Gecko, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple, institutions have another path towards reducing dependence on a single architecture. Finally, Firefox Enterprise is built to live alongside the systems that IT operations already use. Keep your identity provider. Keep your SIEM. Keep your MDM. Just add a browser whose management infrastructure you operate, so you decide where data lives and have greater visibility into how it moves. For us, supporting the goal of technological sovereignty comes down to four things: More control. More transparency. More choice. More resilience. Learn more about Firefox Enterprise. We know this territory. Independence isn’t a new direction for Mozilla. We’ve spent more than 25 years building and securing browser technology that intentionally works outside of the dominant architecture of the day. Firefox is used by roughly 200 million people every month and is already deployed across thousands of organizations.That independence has always mattered to the web. Now it has practical value for institutions looking to reduce technological concentration — and dependency — in their own environments. Our ambition is big but simple: make technology independence practical. That means putting institutions in real control of the infrastructure and data they depend on, without asking them to rebuild or start over. Closing blind spots. Defining where policies, access and data live. Keeping core management within the institution’s environment. And bringing an overlooked layer — the browser — under institutional control. Firefox Enterprise is unveiling across Europe with an initial sales focus on France, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Thunderbird Enterprise is also in development, extending this customer-controlled approach to email and communications. We’ll have more to share as that work progresses. If your organization wants greater control over its browser infrastructure, we’d like to work with you. This post is also available in: Deutsch (German) Français (French)

title: Firefox partners with Anschutz Entertainment Group at the Uber Arena and Uber Eats Music Hall in Berlin
author: Mozilla
article_text: Firefox is teaming up with AEG and taking to the main stage at Berlin’s biggest and best indoor arenas. Starting this October, as the indoor music scene heats up and the basketball and ice hockey seasons are in full swing, fans flocking to the Uber Arena, Uber Eats Music Hall, and Uber Platz will see Firefox highly visible around the venue. Berlin is where we are starting, right across the river from our office. See you there,” said John Solomon, Mozilla-Firefox Chief Marketing Officer.
